name: table
simple: A table is Luau's way of storing a bunch of values together, like a list of player names or a list of scores. The table library is a toolbox for lists: add items, remove items, find an item, sort the list, join it into text, copy it, and more.
analogy: A table is like a numbered row of lockers. The table library is the school janitor who can add a new locker at the end, take one out and slide the others over, find which locker holds your backpack, or line them up in order.
whenToUse: Keep a list of things and add to it (`table.insert`)
Take things out of a list (`table.remove`)
Check if something is in a list (`table.find`)
Turn a list into one piece of text (`table.concat`)
where: A built-in library, so there is nothing to get. Works in any script.

terms.table: A container that holds many values. Make one with curly braces: `local fruits = {"apple", "banana"}`.
terms.array (list): A table where items are stored at number positions 1, 2, 3 and so on, in order.
terms.dictionary: A table where items are stored under names (keys) instead of numbers, like `{coins = 10, level = 3}`.
terms.index: The number position of an item in a list. Luau lists start at 1, so `fruits[1]` is the first item.
terms.key / value: In a table, the key is the label (like 1 or "coins") and the value is what is stored there (like "apple" or 10).
terms.length (#): How many items a list has. `#fruits` gives it.
terms.nil: Means "nothing" or "no value". Setting an item to nil removes it.
terms.shallow copy: A copy of the table itself, but any tables INSIDE it are shared with the original, not copied.
terms.frozen: Locked so it cannot be changed. Trying to change a frozen table causes an error.
terms.tuple: Several values handed back at once, like `local a, b, c = table.unpack(list)`.
terms.comparison function: A function you give to `table.sort` that takes two items and returns true if the first should come BEFORE the second.

examples.title: A to-do list: add, remove, find
examples.code:
local tasks = {"Collect coins", "Beat the boss"}

table.insert(tasks, "Find the key")       -- add at the end
table.insert(tasks, 1, "Say hi")          -- add at position 1, others slide up
print(table.concat(tasks, ", "))
-- Say hi, Collect coins, Beat the boss, Find the key

local spot = table.find(tasks, "Beat the boss")
print(spot) -- 3

table.remove(tasks, spot)                 -- take it out, others slide down
print(#tasks) -- 3
print(table.concat(tasks, ", "))
-- Say hi, Collect coins, Find the key
explain: `table.insert(list, value)` adds at the end. With a position first, it squeezes the value in there.
`table.find` tells you where an item is (or nil if it is not there).
`table.remove(list, position)` takes an item out and closes the gap.
`table.concat` joins the list into one string, with ", " between items.

examples.title: Sort a leaderboard from highest to lowest
examples.code:
local scores = {
    {name = "Ava", points = 40},
    {name = "Ben", points = 95},
    {name = "Cal", points = 70},
}

-- return true if a should come before b
table.sort(scores, function(a, b)
    return a.points > b.points -- bigger points first
end)

for place, entry in scores do
    print(place .. ". " .. entry.name .. " - " .. entry.points)
end
-- 1. Ben - 95
-- 2. Cal - 70
-- 3. Ava - 40
explain: Each item is a small table with a name and points.
`table.sort` puts the list in order. Our function says: a goes first if it has MORE points.
Without a function, `table.sort` puts plain numbers or strings from smallest to biggest.

gotchas: Most table functions only work on lists (number positions 1, 2, 3...). They ignore dictionary keys like `coins`.
Do not use `table.remove` while looping forward through the same list; items slide and you will skip some. Loop backwards instead: `for i = #list, 1, -1 do`.
`#list` can be wrong if the list has holes (a nil in the middle). Use `table.remove` instead of setting items to nil.
`table.clone` only copies the outer table. Tables inside it are still shared.

table.clear.simple: Empties a table: every key is set to nil, so `#t` becomes 0. The table itself is kept, so you can refill it quickly.

table.clone.simple: Makes a copy of a table, so changing the copy does not change the original. It is a shallow copy: tables inside are shared.
table.clone.example:
local original = {coins = 10}
local copy = table.clone(original)
copy.coins = 99
print(original.coins) -- 10, the original did not change

table.concat.simple: Joins a list of strings or numbers into one string, with an optional separator between them. You can also choose a start and end position.
table.concat.gotcha: Every item must be a string or number; anything else causes an error.

table.create.simple: Makes a new list with room for a certain number of items, optionally filled with the same value. Good for speed when you know how big a list will be.

table.find.simple: Looks through a list for a value and gives back its position, or nil if it is not there. An optional 3rd number says where to start looking.
table.find.gotcha: It only searches number positions (lists), not dictionary keys.

table.foreach.simple: Old — use a `for key, value in t do` loop instead.

table.foreachi.simple: Old — use a `for i, value in ipairs(t) do` loop instead.

table.freeze.simple: Locks a table so it can never be changed again. Good for settings that should stay the same. Only the outer table is locked; tables inside it are not.
table.freeze.example:
local SETTINGS = table.freeze({maxPlayers = 10})
-- SETTINGS.maxPlayers = 20  -- this would cause an error
print(SETTINGS.maxPlayers) -- 10

table.getn.simple: Old — use the `#` operator instead, like `#list`.

table.insert.simple: Adds a value to a list. `table.insert(list, value)` puts it at the end. `table.insert(list, position, value)` squeezes it in at that position and slides the rest up by one.

table.isfrozen.simple: True if the table has been locked with `table.freeze`.

table.maxn.simple: Gives the biggest number key in a table, even if there are gaps. 0 if there are no number keys.

table.move.simple: Copies a range of items from one list into a list (the same one or another), starting at a chosen position. Gives back the destination list.

table.pack.simple: Puts any number of values into a new list, and also stores how many there were in a field called `n`.
table.pack.example:
local t = table.pack("a", "b", "c")
print(t.n)    -- 3
print(t[2])   -- b

table.remove.simple: Takes an item out of a list at a position and gives it back. The items after it slide down to fill the gap. With no position, it removes the last item.
table.remove.example:
local stack = {"a", "b", "c"}
local last = table.remove(stack)     -- removes "c"
local first = table.remove(stack, 1) -- removes "a"
print(last, first, #stack) -- c a 1

table.sort.simple: Puts a list in order, changing the list itself. By default smallest to biggest (or A to Z). Give a function to choose your own order: it gets two items and returns true if the first should come first.
table.sort.example:
local nums = {5, 2, 9, 1}
table.sort(nums)
print(table.concat(nums, ",")) -- 1,2,5,9

table.sort(nums, function(a, b) return a > b end)
print(table.concat(nums, ",")) -- 9,5,2,1
table.sort.gotcha: Your function must be consistent. If it says both a before b AND b before a, you get an "invalid order function" error. Use `>` or `<`, never `>=`.

table.unpack.simple: Takes the items out of a list and gives them back as separate values. Handy to pass a list's items into a function.
table.unpack.example:
local nums = {3, 7, 1}
print(math.max(table.unpack(nums))) -- 7
local a, b = table.unpack({"x", "y"})
print(a, b) -- x y
